messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

John, a 56-year-old divorced detective of Oceania descent, has spent much of his life grappling with the aftermath of physical abuse he endured at the hands of a caregiver in childhood. The scars from those traumatic experiences are deeply embedded in his psyche and manifest in various ways that have significantly impacted his daily functioning and relationships. The burnt smell that would often permeate the house where John was abused remains an olfactory danger cue, instantly triggering strong physical reactions. When he encounters this scent, which occasionally wafts through the precinct or from neighbors’ homes during cooking, it plunges him into a state of intense hypervigilance. He is superalert and on guard, constantly scanning his surroundings for any signs of threat. These triggers also exacerbate his difficulty in falling asleep as he remains alert throughout the night. John has come to believe that his reactions since the event show that he is a lousy coper, which fuels his sense of shattered beliefs about how the world works. He feels that the abuse happened because of who he is at his core—a belief that intensifies his feelings of guilt and inadequacy. These negative appraisals have made it nearly impossible for him to explain what happened clearly; whenever he tries to recount his experiences, he loses the thread and cannot finish. The intensity of these memories causes him to detach from them, but this detachment only serves to reinforce his sense that he is a bad coper. When John remembers the event, he feels intense rage—often triggered without warning by people who look similar to those involved in the abuse or even by positive emotions, which further confuse and distress him. These memories are not just painful; they lead him to avoid wearing clothes similar to what he wore during the traumatic events. He also avoids other people, feeling that they might remind him of his abuser or the victims. This avoidance is a maladaptive strategy that has worsened over time, leading John to withdraw from social interactions and even professional collaborations. The more John detaches himself from these memories, the harder it becomes for him to process them healthily. His attempts to avoid similar clothes and people only reinforce his belief that he cannot cope with reminders of the trauma. This avoidance exacerbates his negative appraisals about his character and coping abilities, creating a cycle where he feels increasingly isolated. John’s hypervigilance has had concrete consequences in his work as a detective. His constant need to stay alert and watchful makes it difficult for him to collaborate effectively with colleagues or even engage deeply in investigations. He finds himself unable to fully trust others, which has led to strained relationships both at work and in his personal life. What finally brought John to seek help was the realization that his avoidance behaviors were not only ineffective but were also worsening his symptoms. He was certain that his inability to cope was destroying any sense of normalcy he once had. Despite this recognition, he is most afraid of revisiting those traumatic memories, yet he hopes for a way to find some semblance of peace and stability in his life again. Through his experiences, John has come to see how the trauma has fundamentally altered his worldview and coping mechanisms, creating a self-perpetuating cycle that has left him feeling shattered and isolated. He is now seeking help with the hope of breaking free from these negative patterns and regaining control over his life.
